topic: Departure time choice with schedule delay
idea: Departure-time choice as a discrete choice: alternatives are discretised departure intervals around the preferred arrival time (PAT) +/- travel-time range; utility = travel time (from a simulation at that departure time, TT(DT)) + early schedule delay + late schedule delay outside a penalty-free window around PAT (+ habit penalty); logit with Cross-Nested/ordered alternatives since adjacent intervals correlate (Small 1987). Relative choice set for changes: no change, earlier/later by 1 or 2 intervals (Antoniou 1997).
does: Spreads each OD pair's daily/peak demand over departure slots by schedule-delay logit using travel times measured by a headless run per slot, then iterates (peak spreading under congestion).
inputs: OD pair, preferred arrival time distribution, early/late delay weights, penalty-free window, interval length, simulated TT(DT)
outputs: Departure-time profile per OD pair (feeds shape_daily_curve), peak spreading, equilibrium travel time
existing: partial: shape_daily_curve (fixed shape, not behavioural); not_built lists departure-time choice
notes: Late/early delay = max(0, PAT-window-arrival), etc. Deterministic version gives constant-utility plateau where TT slope = -schedule delay slope; add logit noise for spread.

topic: Choice-set generation for routes: link elimination and detour-ratio availability
idea: Route choice sets built by link elimination (Azevedo 1993: shortest path, remove its links one at a time, re-solve) or labelling (fastest, fewest signals, no left turns, most freeway); probabilistic availability rejects paths longer than a random multiple (mean 2x) of the shortest.
does: Improve assign_routes alternatives with labelled routes (fewest signals, no-turn, max-arterial) and detour-ratio filter instead of only k alternatives.
inputs: network, OD, labels, detour threshold
outputs: alternative route set per OD with labels, rejected routes
notes: Path-size and commonality factor (Cascetta 1996: overlap length ratio) already close to what assign_routes does; commonality factor is a cheap alternative.

topic: Route choice attributes: perception, information access, value of time classes
idea: Route choice depends on value-of-time class (low/med/high), access to information (informed vs uninformed drivers), trip purpose; travel time perceived as random variable; travel-time variability as attribute.
does: Mark a share of vehicles as informed (see live link times, re-route) vs uninformed (habitual route) to test ITS/information policies in experiments.
inputs: informed share, VOT classes
outputs: results by class
notes: Placeholder-level; needs dynamic re-routing.

topic: Prism-constrained tour generation for institutions
idea: PCATS: divide the day into blocked periods (fixed activities such as work/shift) and open periods; fill open periods sequentially with flexible activity episodes (type, duration, location, mode) inside a space-time prism (reachable set given available time and speed). CATGW anchors on work arrival/departure and generates tours before work, midday and after home arrival. Durations via Weibull hazard (duration dependence).
does: Give each simulated person from an institution a daily tour (home-work-stops-home) with dwell times, so demand has linked trips, realistic peak shapes and midday/PM trips instead of independent OD flows.
inputs: institution shifts, population, open-period rules, dwell-time Weibull parameters, speed for prism
outputs: time-stamped trip list per person; hourly OD flows
notes: Also shows trip-based models overstate mode shift for people making stops on the commute; telecommuting/work-time shifts relocate peaks. Keep as placeholder-level unless asked.

topic: Speed-power safety model for speed-limit what-ifs
idea: Crash risk scales roughly with travel speed, injury risk with speed squared, fatality risk with speed to the fourth (Evans). Worked check: mean speed 63.4 -> 57.6 mph predicts -32% fatality risk vs 34% observed; casualty crash risk doubles per +5 km/h (Kloeden). Also: doubling vehicle mass halves occupant risk (mixed-mass crash severity).
does: Given a speed-limit change (or measured speed shifts from two runs), predicts relative crash, injury and fatality risk as (v2/v1)^1, ^2, ^4 and weights conflicts from analyse_safety by severity (delta-v squared) so experiments report expected harm, not only conflict counts.
inputs: run ids or per-road speed before/after, exponents (default 1,2,4), optional vehicle mass classes
outputs: per-road and network relative crash/injury/fatality risk, expected harm change, severity-weighted conflict rate
existing: partial: analyse_safety (TTC conflicts, SPF/EB, no severity model)
cite: Ch4 s4.5 Driver Behavior (speed and fatality risk)
notes: Power model needs a caveat: exponents are empirical. Cheap to add to compare_runs as an extra column.

topic: Fatality rate normalisation by exposure
idea: Safety measures are always rates (harm per exposure: per vehicle-km, per vehicle, per person-km, per hour); choice of denominator changes ranking; occupant-km vs vehicle-km differ for buses.
does: Report conflicts per million vehicle-km AND per million person-km (using each vehicle type's occupancy) so bus/priority schemes are not penalised.
inputs: run, vehicle occupancy
outputs: rate table with several denominators
notes: Rest of chapter is human-factors narrative.

topic: Behavioural-feedback check on safety interventions
idea: Naive model (same crashes, less harm) vs behavioural model: protective technology or perceived safety raises speed. A 3% mean speed rise gives +13% fatality risk (4th-power law), turning a claimed -9% benefit into +4%. Evaluation of a measure must measure the speed change it induces.
does: After an experiment compares two designs/measures, report the net safety effect as direct effect times speed-induced term, flagging when speeds rose enough to cancel a modelled benefit.
inputs: two runs, claimed per-conflict risk reduction
outputs: net relative fatality/injury risk using mean speed ratio
cite: Ch4 s4.7 Airbag mandate and technology/human interface
notes: Mostly narrative; pairs with speed_safety_forecast.

topic: Cumulative curve (N-curve) queue diagnosis
idea: Cumulative arrival A(t) and departure D(t) curves at a point: queue = vertical gap, total delay = area between, mean time in system = horizontal gap (Little's L = lambda W). Deterministic fluid bottleneck passes through four phases: stagnant, growth, decline, stagnant; departure rate drops discontinuously from capacity c to arrival rate when the queue vanishes. Optimal capacity condition (Eq 5.14): optimal queue duration depends only on sqrt(capacity cost / waiting cost), not on arrival rates; an incident at the start of queue growth hurts every arrival over the whole queue duration.
does: Builds A(t)/D(t) per road/junction from detector or vehicle logs, reports queue onset/peak/clear times, phase durations, max queue, total vehicle-hours delay (area), mean delay by Little's law, and checks the two agree; flags where an incident sits in the growth phase.
inputs: run id, road or junction, interval
outputs: cumulative counts, queue-duration table, delay area, Little consistency, estimated bottleneck capacity (slope of D during queue)
existing: partial: read_detectors, analyse_run (95th pct queue per road)
notes: Gives queue discharge capacity directly from the departure slope; useful for calibrating bottleneck capacity and for DEVL/incident scenarios.

topic: Headway variability and bus bunching
idea: On frequent routes (headway under about 10 min) passengers arrive randomly: mean wait = (mean headway/2) x (1 + CV^2) where CV = headway SD/mean (Osuna and Newell 1971); Poisson arrivals double the wait of regular ones; headways are intrinsically unstable (a late bus picks up more, falls further behind and bunches with the next). Control: slow the trailing bus when catching up, at the line start.
does: From bus stop arrival logs compute headway mean, CV, expected passenger wait E[W]=h/2(1+CV^2), excess wait versus schedule, bunching incidence (headway under 0.25 of scheduled), and compare with and without TSP.
inputs: run id, bus line or stop
outputs: per stop: headway CV, expected wait, excess wait, bunching share
existing: none (analyse_run covers trip times, not bus headways)
notes: A TSP agent that only reports bus delay misses regularity; this is the right bus KPI for TSP evaluation. Also lets the LLM justify holding/skip decisions.

topic: Relaxation time near capacity
idea: Newell (1982) relaxation time: the time for a queue to approach steady state tends to infinity as arrival rate approaches capacity, so steady-state formulas are inaccurate near capacity even with small fluctuations; stochastic queue delay is strongly non-stationary.
does: Warn in run_experiment/run_simulation when a junction or road has v/c above about 0.9 that the run length or warm-up is too short for steady-state statistics; suggest minimum duration and warm-up from the relaxation time scale (roughly proportional to 1/(1-rho)^2).
inputs: run id, per-road v/c, duration
outputs: flags and recommended duration/warm-up
existing: partial: experiments report replications needed for a precision, no warm-up check
notes: Cheap guard against drawing conclusions from transient runs.

topic: Spatial queueing for emergency response
idea: Response time = travel + dispatch + queueing; when the system is busy it is travel time that degrades (a farther unit is sent) not queue wait; response distance scales as sqrt(territory area per unit) (RAND/NYC models).
does: Estimate emergency response time versus number/placement of units using the sqrt-area law and busy-unit probability, to complement schedule_emergency experiments.
inputs: area, number of units, call rate, service time
outputs: mean response distance/time, fraction of calls served by non-nearest unit
notes: Fire/police dispatch is out of scope of ACMS unless more ambulances are modelled.

topic: Edie generalised flow/density/speed over time-space regions
idea: Edie's definitions: for any time-space region A, flow q(A)=d(A)/|A| (total distance travelled over area), density k(A)=t(A)/|A| (total time spent over area), speed v(A)=d(A)/t(A) = q/k (harmonic-mean speed, equals the space-mean speed in stationary conditions). Occupancy relates to density through the mean effective vehicle length (k = occupancy / (L_veh + L_detector zone)). Time-mean and space-mean differ (fast vehicles over-represented at a fixed point).
does: Computes q, k, v per road segment and time window from vehicle trajectories (Frame logs) with Edie's method, giving noise-free fundamental diagram points, capacity and critical density per road, and flags where detector time-mean speeds mislead.
inputs: run id, road/segment, time window length
outputs: q-k-v points per window, capacity estimate, jam density, speed-density fit, harmonic vs arithmetic mean speed comparison
notes: ACMS has exact vehicle positions so can integrate distance and time directly; useful to validate Krauss parameters against HCM-type curves.

topic: Active bottleneck diagnosis with shifted, rescaled N-curves
idea: Plot cumulative counts N(t) at successive detectors, shift each by the free-flow trip time to the reference detector and subtract a background-flow line q0*t to magnify; superimposed curves = free flow, separation = excess accumulation. A bottleneck is active if (1) a queue exists immediately upstream and (2) downstream is free; its capacity is the discharge rate (slope of the downstream N-curve) during queue; confirm with cumulative occupancy (T-curves). Persistence from how long the curves stay separated.
does: Automatically locates active bottlenecks along a corridor from detector or vehicle data, reports activation time, queue growth, discharge capacity and persistence, tells the assistant which road to fix.
inputs: run id, ordered roads or detector list, interval
outputs: bottleneck location (road, segment), activation and end time, discharge flow veh/h/lane, queue spill time
existing: partial: analyse_run (queue vs road length), read_detectors
cite: Ch6 s6.2 Locating the Active Bottleneck, Figs 6-6, 6-7
notes: Pairs with cumulative_curves; gives the assistant a concrete diagnosis (where, when, how much) before changing design.

topic: Headway inverse square-root rule and random headway waiting
idea: Optimal bus headway falls with the square root of demand (h* proportional to 1/sqrt(demand)); headway of random batches gives average wait E(W)=E(h)(1+C(H)^2)/2; real-time control can hold or cancel dispatches to cut headway CV.
does: Suggest bus headway per line from demand and costs and predict expected waiting with the headway CV, for the assistant to test with run_experiment.
inputs: line demand, operating cost per bus-hour, value of waiting time
outputs: recommended headway, predicted wait, sensitivity to CV
cite: Ch5 s5.5 Extensions (random cycle length, non-stationary demand)
notes: Bus ridership is not simulated (passengers at stops not built), so wait must use assumed demand.

topic: Bottleneck capacity from queue discharge with sample-size rule
idea: Define capacity as the long-run queue discharge rate of an active bottleneck (counts downstream while a queue exists upstream and nothing blocks downstream), not the highest 15-min flow (HCM), which can be 9% too high (7000 vs 6420 vph in the example). Precision: var(q_hat) gives N = I_d / eps^2 vehicles needed for relative standard error eps, with I_d = var(n)/E(n) the index of dispersion of interval counts (N=400 for 5% at I_d=1); N may be pooled over days/seeds.
does: Estimates each bottleneck's capacity from simulated discharge counts while queued, with the standard error and the number of vehicles/seeds needed for a target precision; flags when a 15-min peak flow would overstate capacity.
inputs: run ids/seeds, road or junction, target relative error
outputs: capacity veh/h, index of dispersion, N needed, comparison with max 15-min flow
existing: partial: analyse_run (reports replications for precision of trip time, not capacity); calibrate_demand
notes: Uses the index of dispersion already computed for arrivals in analyse_run.

topic: Saturation flow and effective green from averaged cumulative departure curve
idea: Record vehicle crossing times at the stop bar over K cycles (time 0 at green start), average the cumulative count: its slope rises from 0 to saturation flow s then falls to the arrival rate; extrapolate the s-slope line back to the time axis for the effective green start (start-up lost time) and forward to the zero-flow line for effective green end; G is effective green; capacity = s*G/C; delay by superimposing the average arrival curve on it (Pitstick 1990).
does: Measures per approach saturation flow, start-up lost time, effective green and capacity from a run, and compares them with HCM defaults (1900 pc/h/lane, 2.0 s lost time) so the assistant can verify the Krauss/startup calibration noted in not_built.
inputs: run id, signalised junction approach, minimum queue length
outputs: s (veh/h/lane), start-up lost time, effective green, capacity, delay estimate per cycle
existing: none (not_built notes start-up lost time 1.8 s vs 2.0 s)
notes: Also gives per-signal KPIs listed as not built (stops, delay, capacity per approach).

topic: Newell simplified kinematic-wave queue predictor
idea: Newell (1993): with a triangular q-k relation (free-flow speed v_f, backward wave speed w = q_cap/(k_j - k_cap), jam density k_j), the cumulative count at any intermediate point equals the lower envelope of (a) the upstream N-curve shifted right by the free-flow time and (b) the downstream N-curve shifted right by the wave time and up by the jam storage k_j*L (back-of-queue arrival is where they intersect). No shock tracing needed. Multi-destination flows need per-destination curves; merge zipper effect 1:1.
does: Analytic fast forecast of queue length, spillback time onto the upstream junction and delay from a link's inflow profile and the downstream discharge capacity, without a simulation; assistant uses it to screen designs (storage lengths, signal splits) before running them.
inputs: road length, lanes, v_f, jam spacing, wave speed, inflow time series, downstream capacity profile (signal green/red or incident)
outputs: queue length vs time, spillback onset, total delay, max storage ratio
existing: partial: analyse_run (95th-percentile queue vs road length after the run)
cite: Ch6 s6.4 A Simple Theory of Traffic Evolution (Figs 6-11, 6-12)
notes: Triangular fundamental diagram parameters can be fitted from ACMS (Krauss tau, vehicle length, minGap) so the screen matches the simulator; validate against simulated queues.

topic: Automated (ICC/ACC) vehicle type with constant time headway and minimum safe spacing
idea: Automated longitudinal control: spacing target = standstill gap + h*v (constant time headway policy, h about 1.0 s or less vs human reaction 1.0-1.5 s), error = spacing error + k*relative speed, with an acceleration limiter and error saturation so lane-change cut-ins do not cause jerk; throttle and brake modes never active together. Minimum Safe Spacing (MSS) = smallest gap that avoids collision under worst-case braking (conservative decel for follower and leader); semi-automated vehicles with a warning-only system need a LARGER MSS than manual (driver relaxes), fully automated need smaller. V2V: vehicles in a 'zone of relevance' ack each other; non-acknowledging vehicles are treated as manual; soft braking propagates up the stream when a stopped vehicle is detected. Lane change allowed only when MSS to four neighbours (lead/follow in both lanes) holds, else aborted.
does: New vehicle type 'automated' (ICC/ACC and cooperative ACC) beside Krauss, with time-headway policy, jerk limit, MSS lane-change check and a penetration-rate parameter in OD/mode share, for testing mixed manual/automated traffic effects on capacity, queues and safety.
inputs: time headway h, standstill gap, gain on relative speed, max jerk, communication on/off, penetration share
outputs: vehicle behaviour in the simulation; experiment results by penetration (capacity, delay, TTC conflicts)
existing: none (only Krauss + LC2013; placeholders list excludes automated vehicles)
cite: Ch7 s7.4-7.6 (constant time headway, MSS, lane-change safe region Fig 7-15)
notes: Behaviour must follow reverse_engineering notes; SUMO has ACC/CACC models as vTypes. Keep as vehicle-type extension, validated against string stability result.

topic: Mixed-traffic capacity by penetration rate
idea: Average headway of mixed traffic with automated share a: no communication, H = a*H_A + (1-a)*H_M, throughput = 3600/H; with communication, the four leader-follower pair probabilities P(A,A)=a^2, P(A,M)=a(1-a), P(M,A)=(1-a)a, P(M,M)=(1-a)^2 weight H(A,A), H(A,M), H(M,A), H(M,M). Manual headway shifted-lognormal, mean 1.8 s (about 2000 veh/h/lane); example automated headways 0.75 s (follows manual) and 0.61 s (follows automated with V2V) at 55 mph from MSS with 0.9g lead braking vs 0.75g follower.
does: Closed-form capacity curve vs share of a vehicle type (automated, trucks, buses) using leader-follower pair probabilities and per-pair headways, and a check of the simulated capacity against it.
inputs: share a, headways per pair, speed
outputs: throughput vs penetration, expected gains, simulated vs analytic comparison
notes: Same pair-probability method applies to truck/car mixes with PCE/headway data; ties to PCU placeholder in not_built.

topic: String stability test of the car-following model
idea: A following model is string stable if the impulse response of the error-propagation transfer function has L1 norm at most 1 (perturbation not amplified upstream). Pipes (reaction-delay) model is NOT string stable; optimal-control and look-ahead models are; constant time headway ICC is; constant-spacing needs V2V. Test: lead vehicle accelerates/decelerates (0.35g to 24.5 m/s, decel 0.3g to 14.5, accel 0.25g) and observe amplification down a 10-vehicle string; automated vehicle filters transients at the cost of transient position error; total travel time unchanged.
does: Runs a platoon of N vehicles of a given type behind a scripted leader disturbance in a headless run and reports speed-perturbation amplification ratio per vehicle (peak speed deviation of vehicle i / vehicle 1), whether the string is stable, wave propagation speed and whether it triggers a phantom jam; useful for tuning Krauss sigma/tau and checking new vehicle types.
inputs: vehicle type, platoon size, leader speed profile, initial headway
outputs: amplification factors, stable/unstable flag, stop-and-go onset, extra stops
notes: Krauss with sigma>0 is stochastic; need several seeds. Gives a behavioural validation (time headway, stop-and-go) separate from detector calibration.

topic: Modal emissions and fuel estimate from trajectories
idea: Emissions and fuel computed second-by-second from speed, acceleration and grade by operating mode (idle, cruise, accel/decel levels) with a modal model (CMEM); smoothing transients lowers HC, CO, NOx and fuel in the 10-vehicle accel scenario (Tables 7-3, 7-4).
does: Adds fuel, CO2 and NOx per run/road from vehicle speed and acceleration traces with a simple modal (VSP-style) model so experiments (signals, TSP, DEVL) report environmental effect.
inputs: run trajectories (speed, accel), vehicle class
outputs: fuel and emissions totals, per vehicle-km, per road
cite: Ch7 s7.8 Fuel Consumption and Pollution
notes: CMEM coefficients not in text; use an openly published simple model (e.g. VSP bins) and cite it. Check later chapters/other sources for a formula.

topic: Total time spent equals time-weighted exit flows
idea: Total time spent in network TTS = sum_k T*N(k); by vehicle conservation N(k+1)=N(k)+T(d(k)-e(k)) so minimising TTS is equivalent to maximising sum_k (K-k)*e(k) (earlier exits are worth more), independent of demand d; no need for per-vehicle travel times and valid with queues outside the network if boundary queues counted.
does: Reports TTS (vehicle-hours) and the exit-flow form as a single objective for optimise_signals, run_experiment and TSP/DEVL agent comparisons, counting vehicles waiting to enter (source queue) so metering does not look free.
inputs: run id, interval
outputs: TTS, vehicle-hours delay vs free flow, exit-weighted score
notes: Careful about vehicles that cannot enter because the source is blocked (SUMO insertion backlog).

topic: ALINEA ramp metering at interchange on-ramps
idea: Closed-loop local ramp metering: r(k) = r(k-1) + K_R*(O_hat - O_out(k)), with O_hat typically the critical occupancy at the freeway section downstream of the merge, r bounded by [r_min, r_max] before reuse (anti wind-up); convert to green g = r*c/s per cycle or red time for one-car-per-green; ramp-queue override when the on-ramp queue detector is occupied. The demand-capacity strategy (r = q_cap - q_in, drop to r_min if downstream occupancy is over critical) is open-loop and cruder. Paris Peripherique trial: ALINEA best on total travel time, waiting, TTS, mean speed and mean congestion duration. Multivariable METALINE only better for incidents.
does: Adds ramp metering signals at build_interchange on-ramps with ALINEA (or demand-capacity) control from a downstream detector, evaluable by run_experiment with TTT/TWT/TTS/mean-speed/congestion-duration KPIs and by the LLM agents as a new control they can tune.
inputs: on-ramp road, downstream detector section, set occupancy (default critical), gain K_R, r_min, r_max, queue override length
outputs: metered ramp flow time series, freeway occupancy, TTT/TWT/TTS comparison, ramp queue spill check
cite: Ch8 s8.3 Reactive Ramp Metering (Eq 8.13-8.16, Table 8-1)
notes: Needs the signal_override hook for non-junction metering and occupancy from detectors; fits the TSP/DEVL agent framework as a third control.

topic: Actuated signals: vehicle-interval and Miller switching criterion
idea: Traffic-responsive isolated control: vehicle-interval method (minimum green, then a critical interval CI after each detection extends green until max green; otherwise go to the next stage; optionally weigh antagonistic demand). Miller (1963) / MOVA: every T=2 s evaluate time wins and losses over all approaches if the switch is postponed by T; combine into criterion J; switch now if J<0 else postpone.
does: A new set_signal_timing method 'actuated' (gap-out/extension, min/max green) and 'miller' (time-win/loss rule every 2 s), so the assistant can compare fixed, adaptive, actuated and TSP-modified signals; the TSP agent then overrides actuated plans.
inputs: detector positions, minimum green, critical interval (gap), maximum green, T
outputs: stage switching decisions each step; run results versus fixed-time
existing: none (not_built: actuated signals, SCATS tactical control)
cite: Ch8 s8.2 Isolated Intersection Control: Traffic-responsive strategies
notes: Lowest-hanging missing signal type; must keep amber/all-red safe.

topic: SIGSET/SIGCAP: stage-based capacity-constraint optimisation of splits and cycle
idea: For given stages choose splits and cycle c: capacity constraint for each stream j: sum_i(delta_ji * s_j * g_i) >= d_j; SIGSET minimises Webster total delay under it (nonlinear program); SIGCAP maximises a demand multiplier mu with mu*d_j feasible (an LP) giving the reserve capacity, always at the maximum allowed cycle; margins give spare capacity. Phase-based (Improta-Cantarella) also optimises staging by MILP.
does: Computes each signalised junction's practical reserve capacity (max demand multiplier before any approach saturates) and the splits and cycle that maximise it, flagging junctions that cannot carry the OD demand and which stream is critical.
inputs: junction phases and saturation flows, demand per stream, min greens, max cycle, lost time
outputs: reserve capacity mu, optimal splits, cycle, critical stream, Webster delay at current settings
existing: partial: set_signal_timing webster/transyt; analyse_network (no reserve capacity)
notes: Implementable without an LP library: with one stream per stage it is closed form; general case bisection on mu.

topic: Green-wave bandwidth objective (MAXBAND) for arterials
idea: MAXBAND maximises the through bandwidths in both directions (vehicles passing all signals without stopping within a speed range) by choosing offsets given splits and a common cycle; MILP solved by branch-and-bound; MULTIBAND gives each link its own bandwidth.
does: Evaluates the green-wave bandwidth (seconds and share of cycle, both directions) for a corridor under the current offsets and searches offsets to maximise it as an alternative to TRANSYT stops for corridors.
inputs: corridor road path, signal cycle, splits, offsets, link travel times
outputs: inbound/outbound bandwidth, optimal offsets, stops estimate
notes: Synchro-style offsets already exist; this adds a bandwidth KPI the assistant can quote.

topic: Store-and-forward model for network-wide signal splits (TUC)
idea: Store-and-forward: outflow of stream i over one cycle = s_i*g_i/c while the link has demand (no binary variables), so queue dynamics are linear x(k+1)=x(k)+T(q_in - q_out); then minimise total queued vehicles by LP/QP or a multivariable LQ regulator (TUC, operational in Glasgow) with cycle-time steps; cannot model offsets or in-cycle queue oscillation.
does: A fast whole-network green-split update each cycle that equalises link saturation and prevents spillback, as an additional adaptive method beside scoot/scats.
inputs: link storage capacities, saturation flows, measured queues per cycle, min/max greens
outputs: green splits per junction per cycle
notes: Handles oversaturation which Webster/TRANSYT do not.

topic: Route guidance regulators and iterative UE loop
idea: Reactive P-regulator at each bifurcation: share on the main route = nominal split + K*(travel time difference main minus alternative), truncated to [0,1]; large K gives all-or-nothing; insensitive to compliance rate. Iterative strategy: (a) initial splits, (b) simulate a horizon H, (c) compute path travel times and stop if differences are small, (d) adjust splits and repeat; system-optimal vs user-optimal guidance; rolling horizon implementation. Instantaneous travel time of a stretch = sum of segment length / mean speed from detectors, with predictive correction beyond 10 km; VMS shows travel time to the next two interchanges.
does: Real-time rerouting for informed vehicles: at chosen junctions a P-regulator splits flow by measured link-time difference (or an iterative one-shot UE assignment between runs), with a display of instantaneous and predicted travel times for the LLM agent to reason on.
inputs: bifurcations, K, compliance rate, informed share, detector speeds
outputs: split rates over time, travel-time differences, delay change
existing: partial: assign_routes (static path-size logit on link times, between runs)
cite: Ch8 s8.4 Route Guidance Strategies (Eq 8.23, iterative steps a-d)
notes: Needs en-route rerouting (not in ACMS). Combine with informed_driver_share. Good agentic hook: the LLM chooses a recommendation under compliance uncertainty.

topic: Capacity allocation rules: proportional vs square-root
idea: Minimising total transport cost under a road-capital budget gives capacity proportional to traffic flow when congestion dominates (cost depends on flow/capacity), but capacity (network density) proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of traffic when cost is detour-dominated (sparse networks; Swedish fit). Detour factor falls with decreasing returns as the network densifies.
does: Compares each road's current lanes/capacity with a traffic-proportional rule (from a run's flows) and flags roads over- or under-provided, as a quick design review for the assistant.
inputs: run flows per road, lane capacity
outputs: capacity-to-flow ratio per road, suggested lane change
cite: Ch9 s9.6 Concluding Remarks: Road Investment (Eqs 9.139-9.150)
notes: Stylised; uniform unit costs assumed. Metric families (Minkowski) in 9.5 are not useful here since ACMS has real geometry.

topic: Facility location on the road network: covering and p-median
idea: Classical location models on shortest-path times: set covering (min facilities so every demand node is within coverage time), maximal covering (P facilities maximising covered demand; solve for P=1..n to trace the coverage vs cost curve), P-center (minimise the maximum weighted distance; binary search on coverage distance with set covering), P-median (minimise demand-weighted total distance; optimum on nodes, Hakimi 1964), capacitated fixed-charge. Heuristics without an LP library: greedy adding, Teitz-Bart exchange (within 1% of optimal on 150 nodes vs greedy 7%), Maranzana neighbourhood search; weighting of p-median vs uncovered demand traces a non-dominated trade-off curve (Fig 10-4).
does: Recommends where to put P ambulance/emergency bases, bus stops or depots, or institution doors on the network from travel times: coverage within a target response time, average response time, worst-case time, with a coverage-vs-number curve; the result feeds schedule_emergency, add_bus_stop and place_institution.
inputs: demand nodes with weights (institution people, OD, junction demand), candidate sites, travel-time matrix from shortest paths, coverage time, P
outputs: chosen sites, covered share, mean and max response time, trade-off curve over P
existing: none (deploy_institutions places at random; schedule_emergency takes given dispatches)
notes: All pure stdlib (Dijkstra + greedy + swap). Coverage models are sensitive to network coding: use the partial set covering variants (cover a fraction of demand).

topic: Minimax-regret robust design over demand scenarios
idea: Scenario planning: for each scenario k find the best design value z*_k; for a candidate (compromise) design the regret in scenario k is its objective minus z*_k; choose the design minimising the maximum regret or the expected regret; plain minimax regret lets one extreme scenario dominate, so use the p-minimax regret over a reliability set of scenarios holding probability at least alpha (Daskin 1997); also maximise the number of scenarios in which a target level is met. Use 3-6 scenarios including the most probable.
does: Takes run_experiment results for several designs under several demand scenarios (peak, off-peak, incident, event) and reports each design's regret per scenario, maximum regret, expected regret, alpha-reliable regret and the number of scenarios meeting a target, and recommends the robust design rather than the best on average.
inputs: experiment id with scenarios by design (or a design x demand grid), scenario probabilities (optional), target level, alpha
outputs: regret table, minimax and expected regret rank, robust recommendation
existing: partial: run_experiment/compare_runs (paired t-tests per scenario, no regret across demand scenarios)
notes: Needs a design x demand-level grid; ACMS scale_demand makes demand scenarios cheap.

topic: Expected covering with busy servers (emergency units)
idea: Probabilistic covering: each server is busy with probability q; maximum expected covering maximises demands covered by an available unit; require b coverages so a node is covered with probability alpha (b = ceil(log(1-alpha)/log q)); M/G/s-loss queue gives the number of units needed for coverage probability alpha; Larson hypercube model tracks busy/idle states of N servers exactly; one facility with queueing: optimum at the median for small demand, moves away as demand grows.
does: For schedule_emergency scenarios, estimates the probability that a call finds an available vehicle within the time standard, units needed for a target reliability from the call rate and service time (Erlang loss), and the effect of busy units on the response time.
inputs: call rate per hour, service time, units, travel-time map, time standard
outputs: availability probability, expected coverage, units needed, backup coverage
cite: Ch10 s10.5 Probabilistic and Queuing-based location models
notes: Only meaningful if several emergency vehicles are modelled; ACMS dispatches single scheduled emergency runs.

topic: Equilibrium route assignment (Wardrop UE) by successive averages with relative-gap stopping
idea: Wardrop first principle: all used routes of an OD pair have equal time and no unused route is shorter; second principle (system optimum) minimises total time. Algorithms: Frank-Wolfe linear approximation (all-or-nothing assignment on current costs, optimal step size on the Beckmann objective; lower bound BLB gives relative gap RGAP = (z - BLB)/BLB stopping rule; the quantity sum(used path costs) - sum(shortest path costs) over demand is a simple convergence check), PARTAN acceleration, restricted simplicial decomposition, path equilibration (shift flow from longest to shortest used path, Dafermos). Stochastic equilibrium (logit/probit) by method of successive averages: step 1/n, direction from Monte Carlo or all-or-nothing on current costs; tends to the deterministic UE as congestion rises; logit with fixed costs depends on network representation due to overlap. Link flows and OD costs are unique under strict monotonicity, but path flows are not.
does: Iterates assignment and measured link times (headless runs) with the method of successive averages (weights 1/n) until the relative gap or the used-minus-shortest path time gap falls below a tolerance, then freezes the converged route shares as assign_routes input; reports the gap per iteration and the UE vs free-flow total time (and optionally the system-optimal bound via marginal costs).
inputs: network and demand, iterations, tolerance, seeds per iteration, route set size
outputs: route shares per OD pair, convergence trace (gap vs iteration), UE total vehicle-hours, price-of-anarchy estimate
existing: partial: assign_routes (path-size logit on measured link times, one shot); not_built lists no equilibrium assignment for calibration
cite: Ch11 s11.1-11.4 (Eqs 11.8-11.41, linear approximation algorithm Steps 0-4)
notes: Simulation-based UE (DTA style) needs several runs per iteration; use MSA step 1/n. Gives calibrate_demand an equilibrium basis and critical_links a rerouting step.

topic: Braess paradox check for link additions and closures
idea: Under user equilibrium, adding a link can raise every user's cost (Braess: 6 users, 83 per user on two paths, adding link 2-3 gives 92 per user, total 552 vs 498; the system optimum still uses the original two paths). Evaluate network design changes under equilibrium route choice, not fixed routes, and compare UE with SO flows; the UE-SO gap shows where restricting a link (or tolling) helps. Also static equilibrium ignores spillback: monotone cost functions cannot represent reduced flow with increased time at queuing bottlenecks.
does: Before/after test for add_road, add_slip_road, build_interchange or road closure: run UE assignment (equilibrate_routes) on both networks and report total vehicle-hours, OD time changes (who loses), and flags a Braess-type result where adding capacity worsens total or mean time, and shows the UE-vs-SO gap.
inputs: base network, modified network, demand, equilibrium settings
outputs: total time change, per OD pair time change, Braess flag, losers list
existing: partial: run_experiment (design comparison with fixed assignment/route choice)
cite: Ch11 s11.8 Fixed Demand Case (Braess example); s11.6 limits of static models
notes: Depends on equilibrate_routes; also the mesoscopic/hybrid DTA discussion (s11.7) matches ACMS's simulation-based loading.

topic: Marginal-cost congestion tolls and cheaper toll designs
idea: System-optimal flows are the user equilibrium under marginal social cost tolls tau_a = x_a * dc_a/dx_a on every link (expensive: tolls on four of five arcs in Braess, revenue 40% of system cost). All first-best toll sets satisfy a linear system (Hearn-Ramana): choose among them by secondary objective: MINSYS (least total charges, nonnegative), MINMAX (smallest maximum toll), MINTB (fewest toll booths), MINREV/Robin Hood (zero net revenue, subsidies). Elastic demand: all first-best toll sets collect the same revenue. Second-best (tolls only on some links) is a bilevel MPEC; tolling only 3 arcs got within 0.3% of the optimum at half the revenue.
does: Computes marginal-cost link tolls from a run's flows and BPR-like volume-delay fit, tests them by re-running equilibrium (equilibrate_routes) with a toll term in route cost (value-of-time conversion), and reports the total-time saving and revenue; second-best variant restricted to chosen roads (cordon or a single corridor).
inputs: equilibrium flows, link delay function, tollable roads, value of time, objective (MINSYS, MINMAX, MINTB)
outputs: toll per road, expected time saving, revenue, number of toll points
cite: Ch11 s11.8 Congestion Toll Pricing (MSCP, MINSYS/MINMAX/MINTB, second-best MPEC)
notes: A policy/what-if tool; requires equilibrate_routes first and a tolled-route response in assign_routes; value of time per vehicle type.

topic: Gravity trip distribution with deterrence function, balancing and Poisson calibration
idea: Flow T_ij = O_i^a * D_j^b * f(c_ij) with deterrence f exponential exp(-beta c) (fits short urban trips, scale dependent) or power c^-beta (long distance, blows up at small c) or Box-Cox generalisation (b=0 power, b=1 exponential) estimated by maximum likelihood; step-function deterrence by cost class. Unconstrained models make flows grow faster than stocks (1% more population gives about 2% more flow) so use balancing factors: A_i, B_j solved iteratively (Furness/IPF) for the doubly constrained model (work trips), production-constrained (shopping), attraction-constrained (school, hospital). Estimate with OLS on logs plus origin constants (Cesario), Sen-Soot, or Poisson maximum likelihood which handles zero flows. Generalised Alonso model lets totals respond to accessibility with elasticities between 0 and 1.
does: Upgrades generate_demand from supply-demand shares to a real gravity model: balanced (doubly/singly constrained) OD matrix with an exponential or power deterrence on route time/distance from the network, with beta fitted to a target mean trip length or to an observed OD/count matrix by Poisson ML, and reports the fitted beta, mean trip length and goodness of fit.
inputs: origin and destination supply/demand (set_end_flows, institutions), route times from the network, deterrence form, target mean trip time or observed matrix
outputs: OD matrix, fitted beta, mean trip time, chi-square or log-likelihood, balancing factors
existing: partial: generate_demand (shares proportional to supply and demand, no cost deterrence); not_built: power-law deterrence and Poisson ML gravity calibration
cite: Ch17 s17.4 Trip Distribution (deterrence forms, double/single constrained, ML estimation)
notes: Pure stdlib: IPF in a few lines; Poisson ML via Newton/bisection on one parameter. Complements calibrate_demand which fits to link counts.

topic: Mode choice elasticities, value of time and constants calibration
idea: With a logit utility U = ... + b*cost + d*time, value of time = d/b (money per time); elasticity of choice probability to attribute x is b_x * x * (1 - P_j) (own) and -b_x*x*P_k (cross), cost-component elasticity = total-cost elasticity x component share (so transit fares, 100% of the price, are more elastic than car fuel); walking time valued about 4 times in-vehicle time; discrete choice elasticities are nearer zero than elasticities of kilometres; mode-specific constants are needed and are not transferable, so calibrate them to observed shares; a new mode cannot be predicted without stated preference data.
does: After choose_modes, reports implied value of time, own and cross elasticities of each mode share to time, headway and cost, and calibrates the alternative-specific constants so that the base shares match a target split; used to answer what-if policy questions (fare, frequency, bus lane time saving) analytically before running experiments.
inputs: choose_modes utility coefficients and per-pair attribute levels, target shares (optional)
outputs: VOT, elasticity table, calibrated constants
existing: partial: choose_modes (multinomial logit, no elasticity or constant calibration)
cite: Ch17 s17.5 Modal Choice (value of travel time, price elasticity)
notes: Same maths applies to institution_mode_split.

topic: Vickrey bottleneck model as an analytic rush-hour benchmark
idea: N identical commuters with common work start, one bottleneck of capacity s, generalised price = alpha*travel time + beta*time early (late arrival forbidden). No-toll equilibrium: price equal for every departure time, bottleneck used at full capacity throughout, last departure arrives exactly on time, queue grows linearly then falls, rush hour length N/s; total travel-time cost equals total time-early cost, so deadweight loss equals half of total user cost. Social optimum: depart at rate s with no queue (a time-varying toll replaces queue delay one-for-one) halving total user cost; marginal social cost independent of departure time; capacity optimum larger by the factor for second-best. Static link cost is the reduced form of this model.
does: For a bottleneck found in a run (or a signal/merge), computes the analytic Vickrey equilibrium (rush length N/s, peak queue, max delay, total delay split) from its demand and discharge capacity and compares it with the simulated queue to check the simulation and to quote how much delay could be removed by metering or spreading (up to half the user cost).
inputs: total demand N in the peak, discharge capacity s, value of time and early-arrival weight, preferred arrival time
outputs: predicted queue profile, peak delay, total delay, saving available from spreading, comparison with run
notes: Pairs with cumulative_curves and choose_departure_times (same schedule-delay logic).

topic: Marginal congestion cost and capacity expansion rule for design reports
idea: User cost f(N/s); marginal social cost = f + (N/s) f' (congestion externality is the extra cost to others); optimal capacity expands until the reduction in total user cost from one more unit equals marginal capacity cost; with user cost homogeneous of degree zero in N and s, toll revenue / capacity cost = elasticity of capacity cost (so constant cost means self-financing); transit: Mohring model gives bus frequency rising with the square root of demand and economies of density; second-best rules (Ramsey pricing, uniform peak toll) not simple to automate.
does: For an experiment comparing designs, converts vehicle-hours and conflicts saved into monetary benefit (value of time per vehicle type, occupancy, crash cost) and shows the marginal benefit per added lane or per added metre of storage against a user-supplied unit cost so the assistant can say whether an upgrade pays.
inputs: experiment results, value of time per type, occupancy, optional crash cost, unit capacity cost
outputs: net benefit, benefit-cost ratio, marginal benefit of capacity
cite: Ch18 s18.2 Traditional Highway Pricing and Investment Model (Eqs 18.3-18.14, Prop. 1-2)
notes: Needs cost inputs that ACMS does not hold; keep as assistant arithmetic over run_experiment outputs.
